Our findings challenge the feasibility of leveraging simplistic methods for detecting uncertainty at inference. More broadly, our work demonstrates how interpretability methods may be used to investigate the way uncertainty affects inference.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Direct Confidence Alignment: Aligning Verbalized Confidence with Internal Confidence In Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we align a Large Language Model's verbalized confidence (expressed in words) with its internal confidence (derived from token probabilities) to improve model transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence, improving transparency. Results show DCA is effective on some model architectures (e.g., Gemma-2-9B-Instruct) but ineffective on others, highlighting the need for model-aware approaches.
papers.conclusion: DCA can improve alignment between verbalized and internal confidence in some LLMs, but its effectiveness varies across architectures, underscoring the need for further improvements and model-aware alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
DCA improved confidence alignment metrics (e.g., Spearman's ρ, mean absolute calibration error) consistently for Gemma-2-9B-Instruct across all datasets.
DCA produced mixed results for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, sometimes degrading alignment and accuracy, indicating the method's effectiveness is model-dependent.
DCA reduced the variance in calibration error (σ_ϵ and σ_M) for most models, suggesting it makes confidence expression more consistent.
DCA had mixed impacts on model accuracy: it increased accuracy for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, decreased it for Mistral-7B-Instruct, and left Gemma-2-9B-Instruct's accuracy largely unchanged.
The effectiveness of DCA appears to be more dependent on model architecture than on the specific task or dataset.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to internal logits to extract internal confidence, making it inapplicable to closed-source models.
The method relies on the assumption that the model's internal confidence (from token probabilities) is better calibrated than its verbalized confidence, which may not always hold.
DCA can degrade model accuracy because the preference dataset includes incorrect answers, and the method does not directly optimize for correctness.
future_direction: Expanding the method to be compatible with a wider range of model architectures.
Exploring more strategies to improve the alignment between verbalized and internal confidence.
Developing strategies to mitigate the potential degradation of model accuracy caused by DCA.
papers.abstract: Producing trustworthy and reliable Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly important as their usage becomes more widespread. Calibration seeks to achieve this by improving the alignment between the model's confidence and the actual likelihood of its responses being correct or desirable. However, it has been observed that the internal confidence of a model, derived from token probabilities, is not well aligned with its verbalized confidence, leading to misleading results with different calibration methods. In this paper, we propose Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence rather than ground-truth accuracy, enhancing model transparency and reliability by ensuring closer alignment between the two confidence measures. We evaluate DCA across multiple open-weight LLMs on a wide range of datasets. To further assess this alignment, we also introduce three new calibration error-based metrics. Our results show that DCA improves alignment metrics on certain model architectures, reducing inconsistencies in a model's confidence expression. However, we also show that it can be ineffective on others, highlighting the need for more model-aware approaches in the pursuit of more interpretable and trustworthy LLMs.

papers.title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention change when fine-tuned? The paper investigates this through a proposed analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for testing hypotheses about how transformer models encode linguistic phenomena, using unsupervised probes, downstream control tasks, and cross-dataset consistency. Applying it to negation scope reveals evidence of the hypothesized encoding in base models but not in large models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a procedure and analysis methods to test hypotheses about how transformer-based models encode linguistic phenomena. Applying this to negation scope finds evidence of an interpretable encoding (in-scope words attend to the negation cue) in BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, but weaker evidence in the large models.
papers.key_findings:
Before fine-tuning, several attention heads are sensitive to negation scope, with the best BERT-base head achieving an F1 of 53.8 in a fully unsupervised setting.
There is consistency in which heads are negation-sensitive across different datasets.
After fine-tuning on a negation scope task, the average sensitivity of attention heads improved over the pretrained model for all four models, but only the two base models improved more than a control task.
Attention heads that had the top F1s in the pretrained model do not have the top-ranked improvements after fine-tuning on negation scope.
The behavior of individual attention heads becomes more consistent across datasets after fine-tuning on the negation task, compared to the pretrained model and the control task, except for RoBERTa-large.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses on one interpretable way of encoding negation scope knowledge, but there could be many other ways.
The study uses a single nonlinguistic control task, but one could imagine exploring a gradient of fine-tuning tasks.
The analysis focuses primarily on the attention mechanism, but does not explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to.
future_direction: Explore other hypothesized encodings of negation scope, such as a tree of attention leading to the negation cue.
Explore attention head changes with a gradient of fine-tuning tasks that are more or less relevant to the linguistic phenomenon.
Explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to, since these form the outputs and are more directly tied to classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: Uncertainty Unveiled: Can Exposure to More In-context Examples Mitigate Uncertainty for Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: How does increasing the number of in-context examples influence the predictive uncertainty of large language models in in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Additional in-context examples reduce total uncertainty in LLMs by injecting task-specific knowledge, which primarily diminishes epistemic uncertainty and enhances performance.
papers.conclusion: Additional examples reduce uncertainty by integrating task-specific knowledge, primarily through reducing epistemic uncertainty, and many-shot ICL increases model confidence by reallocating logit mass and enlarging the logit margin.
papers.key_findings:
Additional in-context examples reduce total uncertainty (TU) in both simple and complex tasks.
The reduction in TU is primarily driven by a decrease in epistemic uncertainty (EU).
For complex tasks, the benefits of many-shot ICL only emerge after addressing the increased noise and uncertainty from longer inputs.
Many-shot ICL enables LLMs to concentrate more logit mass on the correct answer and amplify the disparity between correct and incorrect options.
The quality of uncertainty measures (as indicated by AUROC) remains high across different shot counts.
papers.limitation:
Exclusion of open-ended tasks such as summarization and translation due to lack of robust uncertainty quantification techniques.
Limited exploration of other ICL paradigms like unsupervised ICL, reinforced ICL, and chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Applying uncertainty quantification methodologies to open-ended generative tasks.
Extending uncertainty analysis to reasoning-intensive contexts like chain-of-thought prompting.
Broadening the applicability of ICL in high-stakes domains.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in handling long sequences have facilitated the exploration of long-context in-context learning (ICL). While much of the existing research emphasizes performance improvements driven by additional in-context examples, the influence on the trustworthiness of generated responses remains underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how increased examples influence predictive uncertainty, an essential aspect in trustworthiness. We begin by systematically quantifying the uncertainty of ICL with varying shot counts, analyzing the impact of example quantity. Through uncertainty decomposition, we introduce a novel perspective on performance enhancement, with a focus on epistemic uncertainty (EU). Our results reveal that additional examples reduce total uncertainty in both simple and complex tasks by injecting task-specific knowledge, thereby diminishing EU and enhancing performance. For complex tasks, these advantages emerge only after addressing the increased noise and uncertainty associated with longer inputs. Finally, we explore the evolution of internal confidence across layers, unveiling the mechanisms driving the reduction in uncertainty.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: Can LLMs Detect Their Confabulations? Estimating Reliability in Uncertainty-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How does in-context information influence model behavior and response uncertainty, and can uncertainty signals be used to predict response reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a context-controlled evaluation framework to study how context quality affects LLM responses, shows that token-level uncertainty can misalign with correctness under misleading context, and proposes a probing-based method using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation for improved reliability detection.
papers.conclusion: Providing accurate context improves model accuracy and confidence, while misleading context leads to confidently incorrect outputs, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. The probing-based approach using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation improves reliability detection over uncertainty-only baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Correct context improves both answer accuracy and model confidence.
Misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses.
Token-level uncertainty does not always align with correctness, particularly under misleading context.
Probing classifiers using aggregated hidden states from high-uncertainty tokens outperform direct uncertainty metrics for reliability detection.
Aggregating features from multiple tokens yields better performance than single-token features.
future_direction: Developing reliability-aware generation and context validation/filtering mechanisms for multi-turn or retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent but incorrect content, known as confabulation, which poses increasing risks in multi-turn or agentic applications where outputs may be reused as context. In this work, we investigate how in-context information influences model behavior and whether LLMs can identify their unreliable responses. We propose a reliability estimation that leverages token-level uncertainty to guide the aggregation of internal model representations. Specifically, we compute aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from output logits to identify salient tokens and aggregate their hidden states into compact representations for response-level reliability prediction. Through controlled experiments on open QA benchmarks, we find that correct in-context information improves both answer accuracy and model confidence, while misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. Our probing-based method captures these shifts in model behavior and improves the detection of unreliable outputs across multiple open-source LLMs. These results underscore the limitations of direct uncertainty signals and highlight the potential of uncertainty-guided probing for reliability-aware generation.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Calibration Meets Explanation: A Simple and Effective Approach for Model Confidence Estimates
papers.research_question: This paper investigates if and how model explanations can help calibrate the confidence estimates of neural network models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes CME, a method that uses model explanations (token attributions) as a regularization term during training to improve the calibration of model confidence estimates without sacrificing accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that model explanations can be leveraged to improve confidence calibration, with CME achieving the lowest Expected Calibration Errors under most settings for two popular pre-trained language models.
papers.key_findings:
CME improves calibration performance (reduces Expected Calibration Error) in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings for BERT and RoBERTa.
CME achieves comparable or better accuracy compared to standard fine-tuned models.
Combining CME with post-hoc temperature scaling further reduces calibration errors.
CME helps calibrate confidence for examples near the decision boundary without changing most predictions.
papers.limitation: The method's effectiveness is limited by the reliability and fidelity of the underlying interpretability method (scaled attention) used to generate token attributions.
future_direction: Exploring the use of free-text explanations to help calibrate the model.
papers.abstract: Calibration strengthens the trustworthiness of black-box models by producing better accurate confidence estimates on given examples. However, little is known about if model explanations can help confidence calibration. Intuitively, humans look at important features attributions and decide whether the model is trustworthy. Similarly, the explanations may tell us when the model might know and when it does not. Inspired by this, we propose a method named CME that leverages model explanations to make the model less confident with non-inductive attributions. The idea is that when the model is not highly confident, it is difficult to identify strong indications of any class, and the tokens accordingly do not have high attribution scores for any class and vice versa. We conduct extensive experiments on six datasets with two popular pre-trained language models in the in-domain and out-of-domain settings. The results show that CME improves calibration performance in all settings. The expected calibration errors are further reduced when combined with temperature scaling. Our findings highlight that model explanations can help calibrate posterior estimates.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Mapping Brains with Language Models: A Survey
papers.research_question: How much evidence has been accumulated for structural similarities between brain and language model activations, and what drives this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper surveys and analyzes the evidence for structural similarities between brain and language model activations, finding that the evidence is ambiguous but that correlations with model size and quality are promising.
papers.conclusion: The evidence for structural similarities between brain and language model activations is ambiguous, but correlations with model size and quality provide grounds for cautious optimism.
papers.key_findings:
Many studies report structural similarities between brain and language model activations.
The evaluation metrics used in the literature vary, and some (like pairwise matching accuracy) are less conservative.
The accumulated evidence remains ambiguous, but there are positive correlations with model size and quality.
Larger and better language models tend to align better with neural responses.
The alignment may be driven by shallow processing characteristics or deeper linguistic factors, but it's unclear.
papers.limitation:
The accumulated evidence remains ambiguous.
Past studies have relied on permissible (pairwise matching accuracy) and ambiguous (Pearson correlation) performance metrics.
Past studies have relied on small-sized datasets.
future_direction: Explore various ways effect sizes can be computed across these studies.
Conduct a meta-analysis of the above studies.
Develop linguistically-transparent models to better understand the alignment.
papers.abstract: Over the years, many researchers have seemingly made the same observation: Brain and language model activations exhibit some structural similarities, enabling linear partial mappings between features extracted from neural recordings and computational language models. In an attempt to evaluate how much evidence has been accumulated for this observation, we survey over 30 studies spanning 10 datasets and 8 metrics. How much evidence has been accumulated, and what, if anything, is missing before we can draw conclusions? Our analysis of the evaluation methods used in the literature reveals that some of the metrics are less conservative. We also find that the accumulated evidence, for now, remains ambiguous, but correlations with model size and quality provide grounds for cautious optimism.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature to Reduce Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How is verbal uncertainty represented in LLMs, and can calibrating it with semantic uncertainty detect and mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that verbal uncertainty in LLMs is mediated by a linear feature (VUF) and introduces Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration (MUC) to calibrate verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by ~30%.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that verbal uncertainty is a linear feature in LLMs, and calibrating it with semantic uncertainty through MUC effectively reduces confident hallucinations, making LLMs more trustworthy.
papers.key_findings:
Verbal uncertainty in LLMs is governed by a single linear direction (VUF) in the representation space, extractable via difference-in-means.
The mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone.
Inference-time intervention on VUF (MUC) calibrates verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by an average of 29.6% in short-form QA tasks.
VUFs are consistent across different datasets and models, indicating a universal feature.
MUC improves the alignment between verbal and semantic uncertainty, as shown by increased correlation coefficients.
papers.limitation: The method may reduce correctness rate due to noise in semantic uncertainty measurement, leading to unnecessary abstentions.
papers.abstract: LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims. Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

papers.title: Toward Practical Usage of the Attention Mechanism as a Tool for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How do regularization techniques affect the faithfulness of attention as a method of interpretability? Can faithfulness be quantified? To what extent are attention explanations correlated with human judgments?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that incorporating tying regularization consistently improves both faithfulness and plausibility of explanations obtained through inspecting attention weights across various datasets and recurrent neural network models.
papers.conclusion: Weight tying regularization performs consistently well and should be incorporated when interpreting classifier decisions via attention weights. However, more rigorous instance-level testing for faithfulness is required for high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
Tying regularization consistently improves faithfulness and plausibility of attention-based explanations across datasets and models.
Masked language modeling as an auxiliary objective produces mixed results and is not consistent.
Regularized models attribute more attention mass to words that humans deem important, such as sentiment words in sentiment analysis tasks.
The proposed metrics (change in Brier score and mutual information) effectively measure lateral information leakage and vertical information blockage, quantifying faithfulness.
Regularization reduces the occurrence of adversarial attention distributions, making attention a more faithful interpretability tool.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is on average across the dataset and does not guarantee every instance is faithfully interpretable; instance-level testing is needed.
Datasets may contain annotation artifacts or spurious correlations, which can affect the plausibility of explanations.
future_direction: More rigorous instance-level testing for faithfulness is required.
Datasets need to be carefully curated to avoid spurious correlations.
papers.abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) has been one of the subfields of artificial intelligence much affected by the recent neural revolution. Architectures such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention-based transformers helped propel the state of the art across various NLP tasks, such as sequence classification, machine translation, and natural language inference. However, if neural models are to be used in high-stakes decision making scenarios, the explainability of their decisions becomes a paramount issue. The attention mechanism has offered some transparency in the workings of otherwise black-box RNN models: attention weights (scalar values assigned input words) invite to be interpreted as the importance of that word, providing a simple method of interpretability. Recent work, however, has questioned the faithfulness of this practice. Subsequent experiments have shown that faithfulness of attention weights may still be achieved by incorporating word-level objectives in the training process of neural networks. In this article, we present a study that extends the techniques for improving faithfulness of attention based on regularization methods that promote retention of word-level information. We perform extensive experiments on a wide array of recurrent neural architectures and analyze to what extent the explanations provided by inspecting attention weights are correlated with the human notion of importance. We find that incorporating tying regularization consistently improves both the faithfulness (−0.14 F1, +0.07 Brier, on average) and plausibility ( $+53.6\%$ attention mass on salient tokens) of explanations obtained through inspecting attention weights across analyzed datasets and models.

papers.title: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
papers.research_question: Can a language model learn to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language, and how does this compare to uncertainty from model logits?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-3 can learn to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language, and this calibration generalizes under distribution shift.
papers.conclusion: GPT-3 can learn to express calibrated uncertainty in natural language, and this ability generalizes under distribution shift, indicating that models can be honest about their epistemic state.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-3 can be fine-tuned to produce verbalized probabilities that are calibrated.
Verbalized probability generalizes reasonably well to out-of-distribution tasks (Multi-answer and Multiply-divide).
Verbalized probability is not simply reproducing the model's logits.
The model's ability to generalize calibration relies on pre-existing latent representations that correlate with epistemic uncertainty.
Few-shot learning with 50 examples can achieve calibration close to fine-tuned models.
papers.limitation:
The training and evaluation sets differed in label distribution but not much in content and format of questions.
The study used supervised learning, which is less flexible than reinforcement learning.
future_direction: Test whether calibration generalizes to other subject areas (e.g., history or biology) and formats (e.g., chat, long-form QA).
Test language models other than GPT-3.
Explore reinforcement learning for training verbalized probability.
papers.abstract: We show that a GPT-3 model can learn to express uncertainty about its own answers in natural language -- without use of model logits. When given a question, the model generates both an answer and a level of confidence (e.g. "90% confidence" or "high confidence"). These levels map to probabilities that are well calibrated. The model also remains moderately calibrated under distribution shift, and is sensitive to uncertainty in its own answers, rather than imitating human examples. To our knowledge, this is the first time a model has been shown to express calibrated uncertainty about its own answers in natural language. For testing calibration, we introduce the CalibratedMath suite of tasks. We compare the calibration of uncertainty expressed in words ("verbalized probability") to uncertainty extracted from model logits. Both kinds of uncertainty are capable of generalizing calibration under distribution shift. We also provide evidence that GPT-3's ability to generalize calibration depends on pre-trained latent representations that correlate with epistemic uncertainty over its answers.

papers.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
papers.research_question: Does a universal truthfulness hyperplane exist within LLMs that can distinguish factually correct and incorrect outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing the diversity of training datasets significantly enhances the generalization of truthfulness probes, supporting the hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane exists within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings support the existence of a universal truthfulness hyperplane in LLMs, offering directions for future research on hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on diverse datasets achieve ~70% cross-task accuracy, outperforming baselines like Self-Eval and Probability.
Attention head outputs are more effective for probing truthfulness than layer residual activations.
Increasing dataset diversity improves generalization more than increasing sample size.
The universal truthfulness hyperplane is more pronounced in advanced models like Mistral-7b and LLaMA2-13b-chat.
Probes trained on single datasets like TruthfulQA fail to generalize out-of-distribution, indicating overfitting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various fields, hallucination remains a significant challenge. Recent studies have explored hallucinations through the lens of internal representations, proposing mechanisms to decipher LLMs' adherence to facts. However, these approaches often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, leading to concerns about whether internal representation patterns reflect fundamental factual awareness, or only overfit spurious correlations on the specific datasets. In this work, we investigate whether a universal truthfulness hyperplane that distinguishes the model's factually correct and incorrect outputs exists within the model. To this end, we scale up the number of training datasets and conduct an extensive evaluation -- we train the truthfulness hyperplane on a diverse collection of over 40 datasets and examine its cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Our results indicate that increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios, while the volume of data samples plays a less critical role. This finding supports the optimistic hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane may indeed exist within the model, offering promising directions for future research.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language\n Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in neural language models, specifically how do models prefer grammatical inflections and do neurons process agreement similarly across different syntactic structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that language models use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement depending on whether the subject and verb are adjacent, and that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences.
papers.conclusion: The study applies causal mediation analysis to reveal mechanisms behind syntactic agreement in pre-trained language models, showing how neurons are implicated and providing insights into model inner workings.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 and Transformer-XL use two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement: one for adjacent subject-verb pairs and another for non-adjacent pairs, while XLNet uses a unified mechanism.
Larger models have more distributed agreement mechanisms across layers, but do not always have stronger preferences for correct inflections.
The overlap of high-NIE neurons across syntactic structures correlates with human intuitions of syntactic similarity.
Plural subjects consistently have higher grammaticality values than singular subjects across structures.
Adverbial distractors increase the probability of correct verb inflections more than incorrect ones, while attractors decrease total effects.
future_direction: Intervening on groups of neurons and attention heads to see how components work together
Extending the analysis to phenomena such as filler-gap dependencies and negative polarity items
Examining the impact of specific verbs on syntactic agreement mechanisms
papers.abstract:
Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language
models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate
the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies
causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate
the magnitude of models' preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as
whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with
different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across
architectures and model sizes -- notably, that larger models do not necessarily
learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for
producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the
input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of
neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.

papers.title: Evaluating Saliency Methods for Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we identify when saliency interpretations are trustworthy enough to be used in analyses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a comprehensive quantitative benchmark for evaluating saliency methods on neural language models, focusing on the properties of plausibility and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: Saliency methods do not always generate trustworthy interpretations, and future work deploying them should perform quantitative validation similar to the proposed benchmark before drawing insights.
papers.key_findings:
SmoothGrad and Integrated Gradients generally outperform the vanilla gradient method across different model architectures and datasets.
Interpretation quality varies by model architecture, with Transformer models often yielding the most plausible and faithful interpretations, especially for long-distance dependencies.
Interpretations can fail in either plausibility or faithfulness, and both tests are necessary to assess trustworthiness.
Interpretation quality is sensitive to model configuration changes, so trends observed on one configuration should not be over-generalized.
Saliency methods do not generate trustworthy interpretations all the time, and their applicability depends on the specific method, model architecture, and configuration.
papers.limitation:
The plausibility test only concerns words in the cue/attractor sets, not other words in the input prefix.
Test sets need to be constructed in a case-by-case manner, which requires human effort.
The evaluation is limited to English datasets.
future_direction: Extend evaluations to other interpretation methods (e.g., attention) and other sequence models (e.g., BERT).
Extend evaluations to languages beyond English, especially those with richer morphological inflections.
Explore automatic input consistency tests using adversarial input generation techniques.
papers.abstract: Saliency methods are widely used to interpret neural network predictions, but different variants of saliency methods often disagree even on the interpretations of the same prediction made by the same model. In these cases, how do we identify when are these interpretations trustworthy enough to be used in analyses? To address this question, we conduct a comprehensive and quantitative evaluation of saliency methods on a fundamental category of NLP models: neural language models. We evaluate the quality of prediction interpretations from two perspectives that each represents a desirable property of these interpretations: plausibility and faithfulness. Our evaluation is conducted on four different datasets constructed from the existing human annotation of syntactic and semantic agreements, on both sentencelevel and document-level. Through our evaluation, we identified various ways saliency methods could yield interpretations of low quality. We recommend that future work deploying such methods to neural language models should carefully validate their interpretations before drawing insights.

papers.title: Does Deep Learning Learn to Abstract? A Systematic Probing Framework
papers.research_question: Does deep learning learn to abstract? The paper investigates whether pre-trained language models can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) from concrete instances and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a systematic probing framework to investigate abstraction capability in deep learning models and provides strong evidence that pre-trained language models (T5 and GPT2) can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that pre-trained language models do have abstraction capability, as evidenced by the probing framework, and that this capability exhibits specific characteristics such as a two-stage learning process and concentration in middle-layer attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
The training phase exhibits a 'memorize-then-abstract' two-stage process.
The learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads.
Abstraction capability is robust to concept mutations, and more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones.
Generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.
papers.limitation:
Lack of a quantitative metric for abstraction capability
Probing tasks are synthetic and may not fully capture natural language abstraction
papers.abstract: Abstraction is a desirable capability for deep learning models, which means to induce abstract concepts from concrete instances and flexibly apply them beyond the learning context. At the same time, there is a lack of clear understanding about both the presence and further characteristics of this capability in deep learning models. In this paper, we introduce a systematic probing framework to explore the abstraction capability of deep learning models from a transferability perspective. A set of controlled experiments are conducted based on this framework, providing strong evidence that two probed pre-trained language models (PLMs), T5 and GPT2, have the abstraction capability. We also conduct in-depth analysis, thus shedding further light: (1) the whole training phase exhibits a "memorize-then-abstract" two-stage process; (2) the learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads, rather than being evenly distributed throughout the model; (3) the probed abstraction capabilities exhibit robustness against concept mutations, and are more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones; (4) generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.

papers.title: Different types of syntactic agreement recruit the same units within large language models
papers.research_question: We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that syntactic agreement phenomena recruit overlapping units in large language models, suggesting that agreement forms a functional category, and this pattern holds across languages with overlap correlating with syntactic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that syntactic agreement constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces, with shared units across agreement types and languages, organized by syntactic similarity.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax-responsive units are consistently identified across sentence instances for each syntactic phenomenon and causally support model performance.
Different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units in English.
The overlap among agreement units is higher than with non-agreement phenomena, indicating agreement as a shared functional category.
This pattern replicates in Russian and Chinese, with agreement units showing cross-lingual overlap.
Cross-lingual unit overlap for subject-verb agreement increases with syntactic similarity across 57 languages.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on top-n% unit localization may overlook more distributed syntactic representations.
